attribution: Traditionally attributed to the sage Shandilya; actual author unknown
period: Date uncertain; generally considered a late text, perhaps from the second millennium CE
summary: A sutra text of about a hundred aphorisms defining bhakti as supreme attachment to God and arguing for its primacy over knowledge.
whyRead: It treats devotion in the analytic manner of the philosophical sutras, engaging Vedanta directly. It complements the more lyrical Narada Bhakti Sutra.
questions: Is devotion a kind of knowledge, or something beyond it?
Can bhakti be argued for philosophically?

keyTeachings.title: Bhakti as supreme attachment to God
keyTeachings.text: The text defines devotion as supreme attachment (anurakti) to Ishvara, placing it at the centre of the spiritual life.

keyTeachings.title: Devotion and knowledge
keyTeachings.text: It argues that knowledge is subordinate to devotion, a point of contrast with schools that make knowledge alone liberating.

keyTeachings.title: Engagement with Vedanta
keyTeachings.text: The sutras discuss the self, the Lord and the world in Vedantic terms, showing bhakti as a philosophical position and not only a practice.

structure.label: About 100 sutras in three chapters
structure.note: Counts and divisions vary between editions

relatedTexts.note: The shorter and more widely read companion text
Its form and some debates echo the Vedanta sutras
